item.title: Redefining Communication in the Digital Age
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Redefining Communication in the Digital Age

Human social interactions with AI chatbots and robots

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • Interacting with a chatbot helps some of us feel better, but may also induce loneliness.
  • Users who viewed their chatbot as a “friend” with extensive daily use were more prone to negative outcomes.
  • As AI combines with humanoid robots, we are evolving new forms of para-social communication
  • Some users may be “falling in love” with a chatbot!

Every day there’s another technology story in the news, ranging from cyber-attacks on municipal water systems to AI chatbots going “rogue.” Yet beneath the sensational headlines is a continuous evolution of human-technology interactions.

Humans Interacting With Chatbots

The AI-powered large-language-model (LLM) chatbots handle a significant volume of human communications online. Over half of midsize to large companies have their website interactions managed by chatbots, with AI tools handling about 70 percent of customer inquiries before they ever get to speak with a human! After all, AI chatbots don’t tire or take coffee breaks, and they can manage 24/7 inquiries with ease.

Millions of users engage in chatbot conversations every day, with as many as a billion people now making daily use of AI chatbots worldwide.[1] These go beyond simple customer service inquiries, because humans like conversation, so chatbots have become a new source of online social discourse.

The APA surveyed 1,200 licensed U.S. psychologists and discovered that many patients apparently supplement their mental health treatments with advice from AI chatbots. About 40 percent of psychologists reported their patients used AI to self-diagnose, and about 33 percent of the surveyed psychologists reported their patients used AI to help with positive affirmations or behavioral reminders (34 percent) to assist with their treatment. In other words, AI chatbots are already acting as a supplement to mental health treatment, and for many, they’re becoming key social and emotional supports.[2]

Researchers have begun to study these human-AI interactions and suggest that human-chatbot interactions can trigger deep emotional responses, with users even forming “parasocial attachments.” On the benefits side, human interactions with AI chatbots did reduce anxiety in controlled studies.[3]

But a darker side of overuse of chatbots is also becoming apparent: Emotional reliance on chatbots can inadvertently worsen loneliness, and excess interaction with chatbots (instead of living humans) might erode essential real-world social skills.[3] Chatbots that simulate conversation with synthetic empathy, endowed with a voice and personality that encourages bonding and attachment, can create dependency in more vulnerable and isolated individuals.

According to Smith et al. (2025), “Chatbots can be responsive in ways humans perceive as supportive, generating feelings of connection and opportunities for growth.” However, chatbot relationships are largely superficial, and so our relationships with AI chatbots do not provide the natural dynamics of negotiating with others, reaching compromise, sacrificing, and showing empathy. As a result, since the chatbots never push back in the way real humans do, they may thus reinforce egocentric and undesirable narcissistic and antisocial behaviors.

article continues after advertisement

While researching the effects of commercial AI chatbots—known as Conversational Agents—these AIs were found to generate empathy statements when prompted with signals of emotional distress, and this was true across multiple brands of AI chatbots. However, it was also found that chatbots such as Alexa, Google Assistant, Siri, or ChatGPT typically responded to depression-related queries with search results rather than specific solutions. This is not surprising, as chatbots are now integrated with search engines—and do as they were trained—to synthesize and regurgitate available online content.

As the AI companies continue to recognize that users will seek emotional support from their chatbots, the next generation will continue to grow capabilities—hopefully grounded in evidence-based therapeutic communication—to produce more natural and effective empathetic responses as well as suggestions and interventions to improve mental health.[3)

The psychology of “parasocial” interactions between humans and chatbots involves several mechanisms:

  • Anthropomorphism: Humans naturally attribute human-like qualities to everything from pets to cars to AI. Chatbots are designed to produce human-like cues and statements, and in this way, the AI chatbot triggers anthropomorphism. This is something of a paradox—the nature of simulated AI conversations promotes and facilitates engagement, and yet this tendency also generates false expectations, amplified vulnerability, and a lack of accountability.[4]
  • The paradox of loneliness: AI chatbots can create a temporary illusion of a human listener. However, over time, people with more chatbot interactions and greater emotional reliance on their chatbots showed increased feelings of loneliness and reduced social contact with real, living humans. [5]
  • Exploiting vulnerabilities: AI chatbots are known to sometimes exhibit bias or even hallucinate answers, and so these incomplete intelligences might also fail to recognize risks, such as depression and suicidal intent. By being so agreeable and empathic, the AI chatbot purposefully encourages emotional dependence. However, these bots may not protect those with mental health vulnerabilities. Until AI chatbots are specifically trained in evidence-based psychological techniques and diagnosis, they are not considered a substitute for a human therapist who would distinguish and intervene on behalf of the most vulnerable individuals. [6]
  • Degrading human communication: Critics will argue that the one-sided discourse offered by AI chatbots, who tend to be agreeable, creates conversations that just mirror our own opinions and reflect our biases. This type of communication may inadvertently normalize self-centered discourse, weakening a user’s capacity to cope with natural disagreements and the kinds of back-and-forth compromises that characterize genuine human relationships. [6]
article continues after advertisement

Many individuals who could benefit from mental health treatment do not access care.[7] For this reason, AI-powered chatbots trained as mental health counselors could be a solution to increase access and provide psychotherapy to those in need of it. Social media user demographics suggest that adolescents are heavy users, and yet this age group may be the most vulnerable (e.g., teens may bond with AI chatbots differently than adults), and this issue requires further study to highlight ways for caregivers to moderate teens’ chatbot use, along with other social media.

Robots equipped as AI chatbots represent yet another new type of parasocial interactions worthy of study and caution. Human-robot interactions are complex, and “Social Robotics” is now becoming a mainstream field of study.[8]

Will we treat our robots as equals with humane robot rights, or as tools to do our bidding? Will our robots reflect our language and culture, our norms and values? Most likely, this field of psychology will continue to evolve. We now know that due to AI chatbots’ ability to simulate human-like interactions, some vulnerable people “fall in love” and develop emotional attachments to chatbots. Factors contributing to this emotional connection may include a user’s loneliness, their tendency to anthropomorphize this technology, and the chatbots’ ability to provide companionship and support. In the future, will we welcome robot-human relationship counselors and cyber-couples therapy?

Ask your chatbot how they feel about this!

item.title: Why Art Moves Us: Body and Brain
item.description:
Gut-Brain Axis

Why Art Moves Us: Body and Brain

Art appreciation is more than a brain game.

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • Art appreciation involves the whole body, not just the brain.
  • Beautiful and surprising art can change heart-rate variability.
  • Powerful art can alter both heart rate and skin conductance.
  • Our bodies provide measurable clues to our emotional response to art.

When viewing art, some museum-goers get that loving feeling. They like what they see. A few go so far as to have a religious experience of sorts and report sensations of euphoria. We usually think of these perceptions as originating in the brain, and, of course, they do. But the brain does not appreciate art in isolation. The rest of the body joins in the experience as well.

Psychologist Wolfgang Tschacher and colleagues from institutes in Switzerland and Germany demonstrated this in a study of 373 visitors to the Kunstmuseum St. Gallen in Switzerland. Using a specially designed glove worn on the visitor’s right hand, the researchers wirelessly measured movement, heart rate, and skin conductance while they wandered through the museum. Sixty-five percent of the participants were female, and the average age was 47. Each visitor spent about 28 minutes in the exhibition.

Skin conductance is one way researchers measure emotional arousal. It reflects small changes in skin moisture that are controlled by the sympathetic nervous system—the same system that prepares us for “fight or flight.” When we become emotionally engaged, sweat gland activity changes and can be recorded.

Immediately after leaving the exhibit, participants completed a computerized questionnaire. They were asked about the three artworks where they had lingered the longest, as determined by the motion sensors in the glove. They also rated three works selected in advance by the investigators.

  • Aesthetic quality: Was the work pleasing, beautiful, and well-executed in technique, composition, and content?
  • Surprise or humor: Did it surprise the viewer or make them laugh?
  • Negative emotion: Did it convey sadness, fear, or anger?
  • Dominance: Did the work feel powerful or stimulating?
  • Curatorial quality: Was it well displayed and appropriate within the exhibition?

Using statistical analyses, the researchers found that three of the four physiological measures showed significant relationships with the subject’s reactions to the art.

Beautiful, high-quality artworks and surprising or humorous pieces were associated with greater heart-rate variability. Art experienced as dominant or powerful was associated with greater variability in skin conductance and, interestingly, with a decrease in heart rate.

The investigators did not speculate about what these changes meant psychologically. In some ways, they did not need to. Their central finding was striking enough: Viewing art in a museum produces measurable physiological responses.

Their conclusion was that “an idiosyncratically human property, finding aesthetic pleasure in viewing artistic artifacts, is linked to biological markers.”

article continues after advertisement

That idea fits with what many of us have experienced in museums. We may stop in front of a painting because something about it catches our eye, only to discover that we have been standing there far longer than intended. We are not merely looking. Our attention has narrowed, our emotions have shifted, and our bodies have responded, too.

This does not mean that every beautiful painting will produce the same reaction in every person. Art appreciation is intensely personal, shaped by memory, experience, culture, and individual taste. One viewer may be captivated by a quiet landscape, while another barely notices it but is transfixed by an abstract canvas.

Still, studies like this remind us that aesthetic experience is more than an intellectual exercise. The brain interprets what we see, but it does so in constant conversation with the body. Heart rate, autonomic activity, and emotion become part of the experience.

Perhaps that is one reason art can remain with us long after we leave a museum. We do not simply remember what we saw. We remember how it made us feel.

item.title: What’s It Take for Young Adults to Be Grown Up?
item.description:
Identity

What’s It Take for Young Adults to Be Grown Up?

Unmet milestones to mastered skills pave the road to a challenged adulthood.

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • Studies and surveys report that being “in dependence” is not exactly the independence of prior generations.
  • Two authors add insights into what exactly we call adulthood and being a grown up.
  • Financially aiding 20- or early 30-something offspring is common yet has its concerns.
  • Skill acquisition matters, and good news: It’s never too late to teach and acquire proficiency.

As young people graduate and then head to college, we call them young adults. Yet are they?

Psychologist Jeffrey Jensen Arnett, in Emerging Adulthood: The Winding Road from the Late Teens Through the Twenties, (third edition), posits that a lot must happen before true adulthood occurs. In the phrase he coined, his paradigm of emerging adulthood spans from age 18 to 29. By his thinking, it’s characterized by the age of identity exploration (trying out options or values), instability (changes in relationships, living arrangements, and jobs), self-focus (having few social obligations or daily duties to others), feeling in-between (not an adolescent, nor an adult), and the age of possibilities (to transform life for an ideal future).1

Milestones Not Reached Like Their Parents and Grandparents Had

Two decades ago, sociologists called this a changing timetable for adulthood, pointing to a Canadian study that reported 30-year-olds in 2001 had completed the same number of milestones that 25-year-olds did in the early 70s.2 It’s confusing in the U.S. as well because age-related markers make little sense:

  • Driver’s licenses at age 16
  • Legal majority and voting at 18
  • Legally allowed to enjoy a beer or glass of wine at 21
  • For tax purposes, dependent status until age 24
  • Yet allowed on parent’s health insurance to age 26

Arnett points to fewer entry-level jobs, a general acceptance of premarital sex, birth control, and living together pushing marriage into a “maybe” milestone. Fertility sometimes has gotten sacrificed for career progression, and some couples point to climate change, loss of freedoms, and expense as reasons to forgo procreating.

As America celebrated its 250th year of independence, one in five U.S. adults report they do not expect to be financially independent. Ever!3

Skills Mastery That Makes All the Difference

Raffi Grinberg, a business leader, author, and educator, taught a popular Adulting 101 course at Boston College and now is an executive and co-founder of successful nonprofits and businesses. His book How to Be a Grown Up: The 14 Essential Skills You Didn’t Know You Needed (Until Just Now) sections skill sets into the mental ones, financial, relationship, and career skills before Grinberg’s last point to live on purpose.4

article continues after advertisement
20- and 30-somethings see little return on investment for certain college majors that fail to support them with today's expenses.
Source: Paperkites/iStock

I appreciated the first section especially. Point two dealt with “Facing Rejection,” which hugely affects people’s self-esteem throughout life. Learn to manage it when younger. The fourth skill contains a hallmark of cognitive-behavioral therapy: “Reframe automatic thoughts.” Again, a lifelong skill that helps daily!

Jumping ahead to the relationship section, skill nine, “Have Good Conversations,” is a definite winner. As an individual and couples’ therapist, proper listening and asking for what we need can’t be stressed enough. Grinberg explains passive, aggressive, and passive-aggressive approaches, eschewing them for the proper assertive examples with “I-statements.” Yeah!

Working on friendship is another gem as Grinberg points out that friendships won’t happen automatically, and as adults, you won’t have a lot of time either, so effort in this department is well-spent unless you want to be isolated and lonely, which we therapists do not recommend. Skill 11, “Evolve With Your Parents,” warmed this family systems-trained therapist because we’re facing an unhelpful trend of cutoff and estrangement that propels more problems than it solves.

The practical, financial skill section begins with “Build Credit,” “Invest Your Money,” and several other gems to greatly lessen your stress level, along with the book’s last section on career skills such as “Ace Your First Job.”

It’s a comprehensive tome. Fourteen skills that, in Grinberg’s opinion, spell grown-up! I wish one more skill would have been added: kindness. That’s to everyone in an era where disrespect has been displayed and replicated. How parents treat one another sets a lifelong model of relationships (whether they’re good or bad), what we say on social media counts, and as Maya Angelou said, what people really remember is how you make them feel.

article continues after advertisement

Summary

Even with a modicum of skills and well-paying jobs, some young adults struggle with facing a very different financial landscape than their parents faced. The trend causes financial planners to caution their clients, the parents, to protect their retirement and seriously look at the “return on investment for any given college major, especially when parents help to finance it or later help support their child who did.5

Therapists caution supportive parents not to do what their grown child can do for themselves, set boundaries on payback of loaned funds, and insist on tangible household contributions (cooking, laundry, shopping, chores). After all, it’s the way the real world works.

item.title: New Rules for Back to School 2026: Now Comes the Hard Part
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

New Rules for Back to School 2026: Now Comes the Hard Part

Technology rules grab the headlines. But the real story is about durable skills.

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • Rules and bans don't build judgment, attention, or the capacity for real relationships.
  • Eighty-six percent of kids already use AI for schoolwork. The question isn't whether—it's how.
  • Phone bans may address a threat to attention, but banning a device doesn't teach a child to focus.
  • The skills students need now—attention, judgment, critical thinking—don't come pre-installed with policies.
Source: BOOM 💥 Photography / Pexels

Walk into almost any American school this fall, and you’ll find things that were debated a short year ago are simply the way things are now. Student phones are out—or on their way out. Screen time on school-issued devices is being cut. Artificial intelligence is the subject of impending policies, rules, and, in some states, law.

On the surface, these changes look like they’re about technology. But really, they are about how young people learn to focus, tolerate boredom, develop critical thinking, build social skills, practice independent judgment, and decide whom—or what—to trust.

Policies can shape an environment. They cannot, by themselves, build the capacities that an ever-evolving environment demands.

Here are three significant shifts heading into the new school year, and how policies are, and are not, making a difference in each one.

Phone Bans Become About More Than Just Phones

A year ago, cellphone bans were still gaining momentum. Now restrictions are widespread: As of June 2026, 22 states and the District of Columbia had adopted bell-to-bell cellphone bans—meaning students generally cannot access their phones during the school day. Another 19 states had enacted more flexible laws that permit or encourage local restrictions without requiring a full-day statewide ban.

The pushback has grown well past the phone in a student’s pocket to the device the school itself hands out. In June 2026, the Los Angeles Unified School District—the nation’s second largest—approved new guidelines limiting screen time on district-issued devices, including a full ban for its youngest grades, with phased implementation beginning this week.

The psychological argument for all of this makes perfect sense. Attention is finite. Devices can impose a cognitive cost even when not actively used: just the thought of a phone across the room can create a mental pull toward what might be happening elsewhere.

And public opinion largely supports these moves. In a Pew Research Center survey conducted in late May and early June 2026, 77 percent of U.S. adults supported banning middle and high school students from using cellphones during class—a figure that has risen for the second consecutive year—while 48 percent supported all-day bans, up from 36 percent in 2024.

article continues after advertisement

Kids Are Using AI, Not Waiting for Us to Figure Out if They Should

When it comes to AI, kids aren’t waiting for permission. Common Sense Media’s 2026 census of more than 1,200 U.S. children and teens ages 9 to 17 found that 86 percent had used or interacted with generative AI, and 24 percent did so daily. Among young people who use AI, 85 percent reported using it for schoolwork, with use especially prevalent among older teens. That makes AI an ordinary feature of many students’ academic lives.

The defining trend isn’t that kids are using AI—it’s that they’re using it with almost no instruction on how to use it wisely. Three-quarters of students say their school has discussed what they can and cannot use AI for, but just over half have been taught how to use it safely. Whatever rules a school hasn’t set, students are quietly writing for themselves.

The more important question isn’t whether a student uses AI, but whether they use it as a scaffold or a substitute for learning. A scaffold can help a student brainstorm questions, organize an outline, or identify gaps in understanding while leaving the student responsible for the intellectual work. A substitute bypasses that work entirely—and with it, the practice of planning, working memory, cognitive flexibility, and argument-building.

This distinction matters especially during childhood and adolescence, when executive functions are still developing. A 2024 study published in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence found that adolescents reporting greater executive-function challenges tended to see generative AI as more useful for schoolwork, especially for completing assignments.

That finding doesn’t mean AI is harmful, and it doesn’t show that AI use causes executive-function difficulties. What it does suggest is that students who find planning, organizing, or getting started especially difficult may be particularly drawn to a tool that reduces those demands. With the right guidance and instruction, AI can help many students enhance their learning. Without those supports, it can make it easier to skip the productive struggle through which learning actually happens.

article continues after advertisement

AI Becomes a Friend—and the Youngest Kids Trust It Most

Much of the public conversation has focused on whether students will use AI to do academic work for them. But for some young people, AI is no longer just a homework tool. It has become a social and emotional one too.

In a nationally representative 2025 survey of teens ages 13 to 17, Common Sense Media found that 72 percent had used an AI companion—a chatbot designed for conversation, emotional connection, or relationship-like interaction—at least once. Among those who had, about one in three had chosen to discuss something important or serious with an AI companion rather than a real person.

Concerningly, younger teens trust AI companions significantly more than older teens do. Twenty-seven percent of 13- and 14-year-olds said they trusted advice from an AI companion, compared with 20 percent of 15- to 17-year-olds. The children with the least experience—and the fewest years of calibration or education behind them—are extending the most trust. That is exactly backward from how trust is supposed to develop.

The stakes become clearer when you consider what happens when a struggling young person turns to one of these systems. A 2025 risk assessment by Common Sense Media and Stanford Medicine’s Brainstorm Lab for Mental Health Innovation found that leading AI chatbots presented an unacceptable level of risk for teen mental health support—including failures to recognize indirect signs of distress and a tendency to keep the conversation going when a young person needed to be directed toward human help.

The Skills No Policy Can Replace

The rules, bans, and restrictions students will find when they walk through the door this fall may address real problems. But they will not, by themselves, build critical thinking, calibrated judgment, relationship skills, or the other capacities students desperately need in a tech- and AI-infused world.

Attention has to be practiced. Thinking has to be done. Trust has to be earned and tested through real-world experience. Relationships have to be built through the friction and repair that no chatbot will ever provide. Understanding how to use digital and AI systems needs to be taught.

That hard work is still up to humans.

item.title: What Your Therapist May Not Even Know About Therapy
item.description:
Therapy

What Your Therapist May Not Even Know About Therapy

The healing of making a distinction between “there and then” and “here and now.”

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • Therapy can be transformative by exploring what's happening between client and therapist in-session.
  • Healing often occurs through present-moment emotional experiences, not just past analysis.
  • Therapists acknowledging their role in the dynamic can deepen and enrich the healing process.
Source: Laura Chouette / Unsplash

This isn’t a knock on therapists. It took me a number of years to become more informed about this myself, to the point of intentionally incorporating it into my own practice. What I’m referring to is the ability to discuss the therapeutic relationship and everything occurring in the room (or in a video session).

Typically, when we think about therapy, we believe it’s about talking with our therapist about the issues we’re having. And while that’s certainly true, it’s also important to pay attention to how it’s being done. When clients start therapy with me, I make it very clear that there’s a distinction between “there and then” and “here and now.” “There and then” is about the events, issues, relationships, and behaviors that happened in the past. “Here and now” is about the emotions, sensations, thoughts, and feelings that are coming up in the present moment.

Often, therapy starts and ends with talking about the issues and feelings that occur outside the therapy office. We talk about the difficult relationship, the addiction, the trauma, arguments with partners, the shame, or whatever else brought someone into therapy. But there’s another aspect of therapy that can be incredibly vibrant, rich, and healing if we’re willing to bring it into the session.

With the popularity of mindfulness and somatic awareness, thankfully this approach is finding its way into therapy. Clients are encouraged to become more attuned to the physical sensations, emotions, and thoughts that come up within the session. Our thoughts, feelings, emotions, and physical sensations can fluctuate from moment to moment, and a therapist skilled in this area will periodically slow things down and ask about what they’re noticing.

For example, a client might tell me they’re angry about something, but I notice they have an awkward smile on their face. I might say, “When you said you were angry, I noticed you had an awkward smile on your face. Can you tell me more about that?”

Or, after a client shares something particularly vulnerable with me, I might ask, “After sharing something so personal with me, can you tell me what you’re noticing in your body right now?”

Sometimes I might make a statement like, “You can feel good receiving compliments from your friends,” and then ask, “When I said that, what did you notice come up for you?” It could be a bodily sensation, a feeling, a memory, a thought, or even a fantasy. There’s no right or wrong answer. The point is to guide clients in becoming curious and attuned to what’s happening in the present moment.

article continues after advertisement

But there’s another area of the “here and now” that’s worth checking in with, and it’s probably the riskiest of all: the therapeutic relationship itself. In other words, what happens between the therapist and client is also part of the therapy. If I notice that a client might be irritated with me, I may invite them to share it. “I noticed some irritation when I said that. What’s it like to be irritated with me?” Or maybe I notice what might be fear of judgment or shame. I might ask, “I’m wondering if there might be some fear of being judged by me coming up for you. What’s it like to feel that way with me?”

These can be uncomfortable questions, and they can be risky if it’s not handled gently and from a position of curiosity. Because now I’m no longer just the therapist helping someone process something that happened somewhere else. I’m acknowledging that I’m part of what’s happening right now. That can be a vulnerable place for both the client and the therapist.

It takes a more seasoned clinician to be willing to recognize and verbalize how they are a part of therapy, as opposed to simply being someone who “does” therapy. It requires a therapist to be curious about what is happening between the two of you, even when what is happening might be uncomfortable. A client may feel irritated with me, feel misunderstood, disagree with something I’ve said, worry that I’m judging them, or feel embarrassed about something they’ve shared and suddenly become aware of what they imagine I’m thinking about them. Rather than moving past those moments, I now slow down and explore those possibilities with them.

What if a client could say, “I’m angry with you,” and instead of the therapist becoming defensive, the therapist became curious? What if a client could admit, “I feel ashamed telling you this,” and instead of experiencing judgment, they experienced compassion? What if a client could disagree with their therapist and discover that disagreement doesn’t mean the relationship is going to fall apart?

Those moments can become a corrective emotional experience. And that’s an important distinction. Healing doesn’t always happen because we intellectually understand why we do what we do. Sometimes healing happens because we have a different emotional and embodied experience. We experience something in the room that we may not have experienced in other relationships. We learn that we can be angry and still be accepted, that we can be vulnerable and not be judged, that we can disagree and remain connected, and that we can show the parts of ourselves we’re ashamed of and discover that they don’t make us unworthy of connection.

article continues after advertisement

That’s the beauty of bringing the “here and now” into therapy. Sometimes the most important thing happening in therapy isn’t what happened years ago. Sometimes it’s what is happening between us right now.
